editorial_brief.reader_task: For one shortlisted small-business AI use case, draft a practical handover sheet defining what the agent may access and do, what requires human approval, who is accountable, and how to stop it before a bounded pilot begins.
editorial_brief.distinct_contribution: Provide a beginner-friendly, one-page AI agent handover template and a clearly labelled hypothetical example for an agent that drafts customer enquiry replies without sending them. Turn vague instructions such as 'keep a human in the loop' into explicit permissions, approval gates, operating limits and a tool-specific stop-and-recovery checklist suitable for a small Australian team.
acceptance_criteria: Explain an AI agent in plain language and distinguish permission to read data, draft outputs, change records and take external actions.

Include a copyable handover template covering purpose, named owner and backup, approved tools and data, permitted and prohibited actions, human approval gates, time and spending limits, logging, escalation, stop triggers and restart authority.

Use one explicitly hypothetical customer-enquiry example with draft-only access, no autonomous sending, and no confidential or personal data entered into unapproved tools; do not imply the example was tested or used by a customer.

Describe a stop procedure that identifies who acts, how to pause triggers and queued work, how to disable relevant tool access where supported, how to check for actions already taken, and when to switch to a manual workflow. Make clear that a prompt saying 'stop' is not a reliable access control and stopping does not undo completed actions.

Include a pre-handover checklist for verifying actual tool permissions and approval controls with dummy or approved non-sensitive data, including a stop rehearsal; present these as steps for the reader to perform, not completed tests.
Connect the handover to a small pilot plan: record a manual baseline, set time, quality and cost measures, require human review, and define continue, revise or stop criteria.
End the useful task with a completed handover draft and two or three unresolved questions the reader can take to peers.

Keep the business next action separate: after the draft and questions, optionally invite readers to explore MLAI events at /events and inspect a relevant event. State that availability, format and cost depend on the event page and attendance does not guarantee individual implementation advice or replace pilot preparation.

package.article_markdown: # How to Hand Over Autonomous AI Agents With Clear Limits Draft an AI agent handover sheet with permissions, human approvals, operating limits and a stop procedure before your small-business pilot begins. ![Two people look at a sheet of paper at a wooden table, one holding it and the other pointing with a pen, beside an open laptop.](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/mlai-main-website.firebasestorage.app/o/content-factory%2FU05QPB483K9%2FMLAI-AUS-Inc%2Fmlai-au%2Fimages%2Fhero-99d8cfc2-ede5-4f5a-8979-03cf50c8200a.jpg?alt=media&token=0a12fb75-b95d-46d5-af48-abf0fb5d8578) *Draft an AI agent handover sheet with permissions, human approvals, operating limits and a stop procedure before your small-business pilot begins.* ## Quick Summary - **Can you give me an example of an autonomous agent?:** A hypothetical customer-enquiry agent reads an approved public FAQ and creates reply drafts for human review. It has no customer-mailbox access or sending connector; those permission boundaries require verification before launch. - **What belongs in an AI agent handover?:** An AI agent handover records the purpose, named owner and backup, approved data and tools, permitted actions, approval gates, operating limits, logging and stop procedure. Unknown essential controls must be marked “unverified—pilot blocked”. - **How do you stop an AI agent workflow?:** The owner or backup pauses intake, handles queued and active work, and involves an authorised administrator to disable relevant access where supported. Check logs and destinations for completed actions: stopping does not undo them. ## Write the boundaries before handing over the work Before handing work to an AI agent, write down its purpose, named owner and backup, permitted tools and actions, human approval gates, operating limits and stop procedure. Make those decisions specific enough that someone else on your team can tell what is allowed, what must wait for review and who can intervene. The owner remains accountable for the workflow even when the software takes steps without asking. An AI agent is software that uses information to choose steps towards a goal, sometimes through connected tools. In autonomous AI agents, “autonomous” describes the steps the software can take without asking each time. It does not grant unrestricted permission to access information or act on your business’s behalf. Business.gov.au advises checking AI-generated information against trustworthy sources before relying on it. Build that review into the handover rather than leaving it as an informal expectation. ## Separate reading, drafting, changing and acting Write permissions as separate decisions in your handover. Reading means viewing approved information, such as a public FAQ. Drafting means creating proposed text in an approved output location. Changing means editing an existing business record. Acting externally means sending a message, publishing content or making a purchase. These are planning categories, not a claim about how any particular product divides its controls. Permission to read information does not grant permission to change it, and permission to draft a reply does not grant permission to send it. Replace broad wording such as “access to customer service” with the actual account, connected tool, dataset or folder and the allowed operation. Give the agent only the access its task needs. OpenAI Academy’s small-business workshop advises checking the intended account or workspace, providing only necessary information and keeping a person responsible before acting. Its suggested prompt boundaries include keeping work as a draft and flagging missing information. Those instructions express your intent; they do not demonstrate that tool permissions enforce it. ### Make approval a real boundary Name the reviewer and backup, what they must check, where their decision is recorded and what prevents action without approval. For a customer-reply draft, require the reviewer to check factual claims against the approved source and check any promises before release. Record approval against the particular draft reviewed. If approval is missing or the source cannot answer the question, leave the work pending and refer it to the named owner. For a draft-only pilot, keep sending in a separate, human-controlled workflow and do not connect the agent to sending tools. Check the chosen product’s actual permissions rather than assuming it separates drafting from sending. If you cannot verify that separation, keep the workflow manual. ![A person writes in an open notebook at a wooden table beside a laptop, smartphone, mug, and potted plant.](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/mlai-main-website.firebasestorage.app/o/content-factory%2FU05QPB483K9%2FMLAI-AUS-Inc%2Fmlai-au%2Fimages%2Finline-d428681f-89b7-4743-9ef6-b9cbc1d52dd3.jpg?alt=media&token=9835efa3-db6b-44e7-9088-025d6c0e9807) ## Copy this agent handover sheet Copy these fields into an editable document for your chosen workflow. For example, keep the handover as a one-page working summary, with detailed tool controls in a separate, clearly referenced stop record. This is an original planning template, not a legal compliance form or evidence that your tools enforce the boundaries you write down. Replace every bracketed field with a decision or an explicit unresolved issue. Mark any unknown permission or control “unverified—pilot blocked”, and name who will check it. A completed draft records your intentions; authorising the pilot requires evidence that the necessary permissions, approval gates and stop controls work in your chosen configuration. - Purpose and scope: [business task and intended output]. Exclusions: [tasks, decisions and information outside scope]. Workflow name/version: [identifier]. - Accountability: [named owner and contact route]. Backup: [named person and contact route]. Pilot start/end dates: [dates]. Supervised operating window: [hours and time zone]. - Approved access: [tools, workspace, accounts and connectors]. Approved inputs: [specific datasets, files or folders]. Draft destination: [location]. Do not enter confidential or personal data into unapproved tools. - Permitted operations: read [specified information]; create drafts [specified location]. Prohibited operations: [record changes, source-file overwrites, sending, publishing, purchasing and other external actions]. Actual permission evidence: [reference or unverified—pilot blocked]. - Approval gate: [named reviewer] checks [facts, source accuracy and commitments]. Approval is recorded in [location]. Without approval: [hold behaviour and technical control preventing further action]. Any human sending occurs through [separate human-controlled workflow]. - Escalation: missing facts, uncertainty or out-of-scope work go to [person/contact route]. While awaiting a decision: [hold or manual handling]. - Operating limits: maximum run time [duration]; task volume [cap]; retries [cap]; total spending [A$ amount and included charges]. For each limit, record [enforced control or named supervisor and checking schedule]. Alerts alone do not enforce a cap. - Logging: [location and authorised readers]. Record [item identifier, time, workflow version, outcome, reviewer decision, tool activity, errors and cost], without unnecessary personal information. - Stop and fallback: stop for [privacy concerns, unexpected access/actions, failed controls or exceeded limits]. Who may stop: [names]. Tool-specific stop record: [location/version, operator, verified controls for triggers, queued/active work and connection access, and logs/destinations to inspect]. Manual fallback: [workflow and responsible person]. - Restart: only [named authority] may approve after [cause corrected, completed actions checked, pending work reconciled and controls rechecked]. Stopping does not undo completed actions. - Pilot decision: manual baseline [location/status]. Measures [end-to-end handling time, quality/corrections and actual costs]. Human review [reviewer and required checks]. Continue if [conditions]; revise if [contained shortfall]; stop if [critical failure or limit breach]. - Verification and sign-off: permission checks [status/evidence]; approval checks [status/evidence]; stop rehearsal [status/evidence]. Unresolved issues [issue, owner, follow-up date and launch-blocking status]. Draft reviewed by [owner/backup/date]. Pilot authorisation [pending or named approver/date]. ## Hypothetical example: draft customer replies without sending Hypothetical teaching example—not implemented or tested. This completed planning draft uses invented names, resource labels, limits and decision thresholds. They are assumptions for the exercise, not customer results, verified product capabilities or recommended benchmarks. Every proposed technical control remains “unverified—pilot blocked” until checked in the chosen tools. Purpose and accountability: The fictional workflow, Enquiry Draft Pilot, version A, prepares replies about public opening hours and services. Maya Chen is the accountable owner; Leo Tran is the backup. They supervise operation and use their internal team contact channel for escalation. Account enquiries, complaints, refunds and personalised commitments are outside scope. Missing facts and out-of-scope requests go to Maya, or Leo when Maya is unavailable, without an invented answer. Tools and data: The proposed business-approved workflow runner, Draft Runner, reads Public FAQ and Approved Inputs, then creates drafts in Draft Review. These are fictional resource labels, not vendor menu paths. Inputs are limited to dummy questions or staff-written, approved non-sensitive summaries. The agent receives no customer-mailbox access. Confidential or personal data must not enter unapproved tools. Permissions and approval: The proposed access allows reading the FAQ and admitted inputs and creating new drafts in Draft Review. It prohibits sending, publishing, purchasing, changing customer records, overwriting source files and using unapproved tools. Maya or Leo checks every draft against the FAQ and records approval, required changes or rejection in Review Log. Without approval, the draft stays unused. A person may manually send an approved reply from a separate mail application. The agent has no sending connector, and that separation must be verified before launch. Operating limits: In this hypothetical pilot, operation lasts five working days from an authorised start, covers at most 20 eligible enquiries and permits one draft attempt per enquiry, with an A$30 tool-cost ceiling. Maya records the start and end dates when authorising launch. Operation is supervised only. The proposed runner configuration would enforce the end date, task count and no-retry rule; Maya or Leo would control each operating session. A provider-side spending cap would need verification. Cost alerts alone would not establish an enforced ceiling. Any limit without a workable, verified enforcement or supervision method remains a launch blocker. Logging and escalation: Review Log is restricted to Maya and Leo and records the item ID, time, workflow version, draft outcome, reviewer decision, tool activity and cost. It avoids unnecessary customer information. Either operator may stop the workflow for suspected data exposure, unexpected access, prohibited activity, failed controls or exceeded limits. Maya alone may authorise restart after correction, reconciliation of pending work and repeated checks. Stop record: Stop Map A identifies Draft Runner, the Approved Inputs pending-work area, and the Public FAQ and Draft Review connections. Maya is the primary stop operator and proposed connection administrator; Leo is the backup, subject to verifying that both have the necessary access. The intended procedure is to pause submissions and triggers, hold queued items, check active runs separately, and disable relevant connections where supported and safe. They would inspect runner activity, pending items, draft history and billing records for completed actions, outstanding work and charges. Exact control locations, shared-account dependencies and effects on queued and active work still require verification using current provider instructions. Uncertain control or output integrity means switching to manual drafting and review. Pilot decision: Before launch, Maya records a comparable manual baseline for end-to-end handling time, factual quality and cost. Assisted handling time includes preparation, review, corrections and manual sending; setup and rehearsal effort are recorded separately for the overall assessment. The hypothetical continue rule requires lower reviewed handling time, no material factual errors or boundary breaches, and costs within the ceiling. A contained quality or time shortfall calls for revision and another agreed scope. Privacy, permission or control failures require stopping. Continuing does not grant sending authority. Verification and sign-off: The draft is complete. Permission checks, the baseline and the stop rehearsal are pending. The pilot is not authorised. ![An open laptop, mug, notebook, pen and phone sit on a wooden desk beside potted plants and a window overlooking city buildings.](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/mlai-main-website.firebasestorage.app/o/content-factory%2FU05QPB483K9%2FMLAI-AUS-Inc%2Fmlai-au%2Fimages%2Finline-bfc4efe2-5fb8-4867-88f4-0c197da98d3e.jpg?alt=media&token=72cc5271-b7e4-47c6-8947-eed676615664) > ### A stop prompt is not an access control > > Telling an agent “stop” does not reliably remove tool access; use verified workflow and account controls. Stopping does not undo completed actions, so record what happened and what recovery requires. ## Write the stop procedure for your actual tools Write down which person will operate the actual workflow and account controls, and how they will check the result. Attach a compact stop map to the handover for each connected tool. Record its tool and workflow identifier, responsible operator and required access, verified control location, treatment of queued and active work, connection-disable method, evidence to inspect, manual fallback and restart condition. This guide provides a planning checklist, not vendor-specific stop instructions. Fill in these details from your administration screens and current provider instructions, then verify them before launch. If a necessary control remains unverified, keep the workflow manual. ### Pause and isolate The owner or backup should record the stop trigger and time, then pause new manual submissions, schedules and event triggers. Hold or cancel queued work using the controls documented in the stop map. Check active runs separately and establish whether the tool supports cancelling them. Do not treat paused intake as evidence that work already running has stopped. The authorised administrator should then disable the relevant workflow connection, integration account or access credential where the product supports it and it is safe to do so. Identify shared-account dependencies before the pilot so the administrator knows what else a change could interrupt. Verify the effect in the connected tools rather than assuming that revoking access instantly cancels every operation. ### Check and recover Inspect available workflow logs and destination tools for completed actions, outstanding jobs, duplicate work and charges. Preserve the incident record, including what the operator checked and found. Where logs are incomplete, record the uncertainty and escalate it to the accountable owner rather than concluding that nothing happened. Switch to the documented manual workflow whenever control or output integrity is uncertain. Any correction of a completed action needs its own authorisation. Restart only after the cause has been addressed and pending work has been reconciled. Repeat the relevant permission and stop checks, and obtain approval from the named restart authority before resuming. Record that decision in the handover. ## Verify the controls before handing over Ask your administrator to show what actually prevents an unapproved action, and confirm that the owner and backup can access the controls they are expected to operate. Use dummy or approved non-sensitive data in an isolated test setting for permission checks and the stop rehearsal. Do not attempt prohibited actions against real customers, live business records or payment destinations. Keep a verification record alongside the handover. Describe what you observed rather than simply writing ‘passed’, and assign each unresolved issue to someone who can follow it up. A successful rehearsal provides limited evidence for that configuration, not a safety guarantee. ### Four checks to perform before handover 1. Inspect accounts, connector permissions, data locations and approval settings with the owner and backup. Compare actual access with the handover sheet. 2. Check drafting, out-of-scope escalation and withheld approval using dummy or approved non-sensitive inputs in an isolated setting. Verify that sending and record changes are unavailable; non-execution alone does not prove access is denied. 3. Rehearse the stop record: pause intake, hold queued work, check active runs and disable relevant connections where supported and safe. Inspect logs and destinations, and record any limitations. 4. Record the tool and workflow version, date, checker, expected behaviour and observed results. Resolve discrepancies and obtain named pilot authorisation before launch. Keep the workflow manual if any necessary control remains unverified. ## Connect the handover to a bounded pilot Before the pilot begins, record how your team handles comparable eligible tasks manually: end-to-end handling time, corrections or quality issues, and relevant costs. This is your baseline for deciding whether the assisted workflow helps. For the customer-enquiry teaching example, the baseline still needs to be measured; no time saving has been established. Add the pilot end date, task-volume ceiling, supervised operating window and budget in A$ to the handover. For each limit, record whether the tool stops execution or merely alerts someone. An alert needs a named person to act on it and is not an enforced spending cap. Measure the whole assisted workflow, not just how quickly the agent produces text. Include preparing the input, checking the draft, correcting it and sending the approved reply manually. Record setup and stop-rehearsal effort separately, then include that effort in the overall pilot assessment. Alongside handling time, log factual errors, corrections, escalations and any action outside the agreed permissions. Track actual tool costs, including relevant subscription and usage charges. Keep human review throughout: a draft-only pilot still requires someone to check every reply against the approved information before using it. Write the continue, revise and stop rules before launch, so faster drafting cannot quietly outweigh a control failure. Continue only when the agreed time, quality and cost conditions are met and no critical issue remains unresolved. Revise a contained quality or time shortfall by documenting the change, agreeing a new scope and repeating the relevant checks before resuming. Stop for uncontrolled access, privacy concerns, failed stop controls or exceeded operating limits, and follow the handover’s stop-and-recovery procedure rather than simply asking the agent to behave differently. At the review date, use the recorded results to decide the next step. A small pilot provides evidence about that workflow under those conditions, not proof of general productivity gains. If you continue, retain the existing permissions unless a separate review explicitly authorises a change. Better draft performance does not, by itself, justify connecting a sending tool or removing human approval. ![Close-up of a person holding a pen near their lips and looking downward, with a laptop and white cup on the desk.](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/mlai-main-website.firebasestorage.app/o/content-factory%2FU05QPB483K9%2FMLAI-AUS-Inc%2Fmlai-au%2Fimages%2Finline-5867c79f-5547-4a35-bb0b-22c4ca886783.jpg?alt=media&token=c67b7758-e1cc-4b9e-821c-41fe98436204) ## Finish your draft and take three questions to peers Have the owner and backup review and date the handover draft. Take a sanitised summary to peers, with the unresolved decisions clearly marked. Leave out credentials, customer messages and confidential workflow details. Peer discussion can help you spot missing questions, but it does not replace checking the actual configuration with the person who administers your tools. Adapt these questions to the decisions still open in your draft: - Can our chosen tools separate drafting from sending, and what evidence should we ask the administrator to show? - What happens to queued and active work when our stop controls are used? - Which quality failures should stop this pilot even if handling time improves? ## Optional support after the draft is complete You can explore MLAI events to learn alongside other builders and business owners. Check a relevant event page before deciding to attend: availability, format and cost depend on that page. Attendance does not guarantee individual implementation advice or replace permission checks, the stop rehearsal or pilot preparation. If your team cannot resolve an implementation gap, MLAI Studio offers paid AI and software development. Use a sanitised handover to define the workflow, its boundaries and the controls still needed. Studio describes checking whether your existing software can do the job before suggesting a custom build. Keep unresolved launch blockers visible, whichever implementation route you choose. ![Four people sit in a circle, one gesturing, in a bright room with large windows, plants, tables, laptops, and a projection screen.](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/mlai-main-website.firebasestorage.app/o/content-factory%2FU05QPB483K9%2FMLAI-AUS-Inc%2Fmlai-au%2Fimages%2Finline-85481514-0afb-4176-90d3-610761ee3f87.jpg?alt=media&token=8f10c771-5b45-4a5a-9937-be92fd0fe183) ## Next Step **Get in touch about MLAI Studio** Browse testimonials and case studies from MLAI Studio, understand how MLAI Studio works, the price per month and how many builder hours that buys you. [Explore MLAI Studio](https://mlai.au/mlai-studio) ## References - [Artificial intelligence (AI) | business.gov.au](https://business.gov.au/online-and-digital/artificial-intelligence) - [ChatGPT for Small Business | Workshop Resource Hub - Resource | OpenAI Academy](https://academy.openai.com/public/resources/openai-academy-small-business-resource-hub-2026-06-03) - [AI Coding Agents: What Autonomous Agents Do in Development](https://teamvoy.com/blog/what-are-autonomous-ai-agents/) - [MLAI Studio | AI & software for your business](https://mlai.au/mlai-studio)

Unresolved issues [issue, owner, follow-up date and launch-blocking status]. Draft reviewed by [owner/backup/date]. Pilot authorisation [pending or named approver/date].

Hypothetical example: draft customer replies without sending

They are assumptions for the exercise, not customer results, verified product capabilities or recommended benchmarks. Every proposed technical control remains “unverified—pilot blocked” until checked in the chosen tools.

Purpose and accountability: The fictional workflow, Enquiry Draft Pilot, version A, prepares replies about public opening hours and services. Maya Chen is the accountable owner; Leo Tran is the backup. They supervise operation and use their internal team contact channel for escalation. Account enquiries, complaints, refunds and personalised commitments are outside scope. Missing facts and out-of-scope requests go to Maya, or Leo when Maya is unavailable, without an invented answer.

Tools and data: The proposed business-approved workflow runner, Draft Runner, reads Public FAQ and Approved Inputs, then creates drafts in Draft Review. These are fictional resource labels, not vendor menu paths. Inputs are limited to dummy questions or staff-written, approved non-sensitive summaries. The agent receives no customer-mailbox access. Confidential or personal data must not enter unapproved tools.

Permissions and approval: The proposed access allows reading the FAQ and admitted inputs and creating new drafts in Draft Review. It prohibits sending, publishing, purchasing, changing customer records, overwriting source files and using unapproved tools.

Maya or Leo checks every draft against the FAQ and records approval, required changes or rejection in Review Log. Without approval, the draft stays unused. A person may manually send an approved reply from a separate mail application. The agent has no sending connector, and that separation must be verified before launch.

Operating limits: In this hypothetical pilot, operation lasts five working days from an authorised start, covers at most 20 eligible enquiries and permits one draft attempt per enquiry, with an A$30 tool-cost ceiling. Maya records the start and end dates when authorising launch. Operation is supervised only.

The proposed runner configuration would enforce the end date, task count and no-retry rule; Maya or Leo would control each operating session. A provider-side spending cap would need verification. Cost alerts alone would not establish an enforced ceiling. Any limit without a workable, verified enforcement or supervision method remains a launch blocker.

It avoids unnecessary customer information. Either operator may stop the workflow for suspected data exposure, unexpected access, prohibited activity, failed controls or exceeded limits. Maya alone may authorise restart after correction, reconciliation of pending work and repeated checks.

The intended procedure is to pause submissions and triggers, hold queued items, check active runs separately, and disable relevant connections where supported and safe. They would inspect runner activity, pending items, draft history and billing records for completed actions, outstanding work and charges.

Exact control locations, shared-account dependencies and effects on queued and active work still require verification using current provider instructions. Uncertain control or output integrity means switching to manual drafting and review.

Pilot decision: Before launch, Maya records a comparable manual baseline for end-to-end handling time, factual quality and cost. Assisted handling time includes preparation, review, corrections and manual sending; setup and rehearsal effort are recorded separately for the overall assessment.

A stop prompt is not an access control

Telling an agent “stop” does not reliably remove tool access; use verified workflow and account controls. Stopping does not undo completed actions, so record what happened and what recovery requires.

Write the stop procedure for your actual tools

Write down which person will operate the actual workflow and account controls, and how they will check the result. Attach a compact stop map to the handover for each connected tool. Record its tool and workflow identifier, responsible operator and required access, verified control location, treatment of queued and active work, connection-disable method, evidence to inspect, manual fallback and restart condition.

This guide provides a planning checklist, not vendor-specific stop instructions. Fill in these details from your administration screens and current provider instructions, then verify them before launch. If a necessary control remains unverified, keep the workflow manual.

Pause and isolate

The owner or backup should record the stop trigger and time, then pause new manual submissions, schedules and event triggers. Hold or cancel queued work using the controls documented in the stop map. Check active runs separately and establish whether the tool supports cancelling them. Do not treat paused intake as evidence that work already running has stopped.

The authorised administrator should then disable the relevant workflow connection, integration account or access credential where the product supports it and it is safe to do so. Identify shared-account dependencies before the pilot so the administrator knows what else a change could interrupt. Verify the effect in the connected tools rather than assuming that revoking access instantly cancels every operation.

Check and recover

Inspect available workflow logs and destination tools for completed actions, outstanding jobs, duplicate work and charges. Preserve the incident record, including what the operator checked and found. Where logs are incomplete, record the uncertainty and escalate it to the accountable owner rather than concluding that nothing happened.

Switch to the documented manual workflow whenever control or output integrity is uncertain. Any correction of a completed action needs its own authorisation. Restart only after the cause has been addressed and pending work has been reconciled. Repeat the relevant permission and stop checks, and obtain approval from the named restart authority before resuming. Record that decision in the handover.

Verify the controls before handing over

Ask your administrator to show what actually prevents an unapproved action, and confirm that the owner and backup can access the controls they are expected to operate.

Use dummy or approved non-sensitive data in an isolated test setting for permission checks and the stop rehearsal. Do not attempt prohibited actions against real customers, live business records or payment destinations.

Keep a verification record alongside the handover. Describe what you observed rather than simply writing ‘passed’, and assign each unresolved issue to someone who can follow it up. A successful rehearsal provides limited evidence for that configuration, not a safety guarantee.

Four checks to perform before handover

  1. Inspect accounts, connector permissions, data locations and approval settings with the owner and backup. Compare actual access with the handover sheet.
  2. Check drafting, out-of-scope escalation and withheld approval using dummy or approved non-sensitive inputs in an isolated setting. Verify that sending and record changes are unavailable; non-execution alone does not prove access is denied.
  3. Rehearse the stop record: pause intake, hold queued work, check active runs and disable relevant connections where supported and safe. Inspect logs and destinations, and record any limitations.
  4. Record the tool and workflow version, date, checker, expected behaviour and observed results. Resolve discrepancies and obtain named pilot authorisation before launch. Keep the workflow manual if any necessary control remains unverified.

Connect the handover to a bounded pilot

Before the pilot begins, record how your team handles comparable eligible tasks manually: end-to-end handling time, corrections or quality issues, and relevant costs. This is your baseline for deciding whether the assisted workflow helps. For the customer-enquiry teaching example, the baseline still needs to be measured; no time saving has been established.

Add the pilot end date, task-volume ceiling, supervised operating window and budget in A$ to the handover. For each limit, record whether the tool stops execution or merely alerts someone. An alert needs a named person to act on it and is not an enforced spending cap.

Measure the whole assisted workflow, not just how quickly the agent produces text. Include preparing the input, checking the draft, correcting it and sending the approved reply manually. Record setup and stop-rehearsal effort separately, then include that effort in the overall pilot assessment.

Alongside handling time, log factual errors, corrections, escalations and any action outside the agreed permissions. Track actual tool costs, including relevant subscription and usage charges. Keep human review throughout: a draft-only pilot still requires someone to check every reply against the approved information before using it.

Write the continue, revise and stop rules before launch, so faster drafting cannot quietly outweigh a control failure. Continue only when the agreed time, quality and cost conditions are met and no critical issue remains unresolved. Revise a contained quality or time shortfall by documenting the change, agreeing a new scope and repeating the relevant checks before resuming. Stop for uncontrolled access, privacy concerns, failed stop controls or exceeded operating limits, and follow the handover’s stop-and-recovery procedure rather than simply asking the agent to behave differently.

At the review date, use the recorded results to decide the next step. A small pilot provides evidence about that workflow under those conditions, not proof of general productivity gains. If you continue, retain the existing permissions unless a separate review explicitly authorises a change. Better draft performance does not, by itself, justify connecting a sending tool or removing human approval.

Finish your draft and take three questions to peers

Have the owner and backup review and date the handover draft.

Take a sanitised summary to peers, with the unresolved decisions clearly marked. Leave out credentials, customer messages and confidential workflow details. Peer discussion can help you spot missing questions, but it does not replace checking the actual configuration with the person who administers your tools. Adapt these questions to the decisions still open in your draft:

  • Can our chosen tools separate drafting from sending, and what evidence should we ask the administrator to show?
  • What happens to queued and active work when our stop controls are used?
  • Which quality failures should stop this pilot even if handling time improves?

sections.heading: Write the boundaries before handing over the work
paragraphs: Before handing work to an AI agent, write down its purpose, named owner and backup, permitted tools and actions, human approval gates, operating limits and stop procedure. Make those decisions specific enough that someone else on your team can tell what is allowed, what must wait for review and who can intervene. The owner remains accountable for the workflow even when the software takes steps without asking.

An AI agent is software that uses information to choose steps towards a goal, sometimes through connected tools. In autonomous AI agents, “autonomous” describes the steps the software can take without asking each time. It does not grant unrestricted permission to access information or act on your business’s behalf.
Business.gov.au advises checking AI-generated information against trustworthy sources before relying on it. Build that review into the handover rather than leaving it as an informal expectation.

sections.heading: Separate reading, drafting, changing and acting
paragraphs: Write permissions as separate decisions in your handover. Reading means viewing approved information, such as a public FAQ. Drafting means creating proposed text in an approved output location. Changing means editing an existing business record. Acting externally means sending a message, publishing content or making a purchase. These are planning categories, not a claim about how any particular product divides its controls. Permission to read information does not grant permission to change it, and permission to draft a reply does not grant permission to send it.
Replace broad wording such as “access to customer service” with the actual account, connected tool, dataset or folder and the allowed operation. Give the agent only the access its task needs.

OpenAI Academy’s small-business workshop advises checking the intended account or workspace, providing only necessary information and keeping a person responsible before acting. Its suggested prompt boundaries include keeping work as a draft and flagging missing information. Those instructions express your intent; they do not demonstrate that tool permissions enforce it.

subsections.heading: Make approval a real boundary
paragraphs: Name the reviewer and backup, what they must check, where their decision is recorded and what prevents action without approval. For a customer-reply draft, require the reviewer to check factual claims against the approved source and check any promises before release. Record approval against the particular draft reviewed. If approval is missing or the source cannot answer the question, leave the work pending and refer it to the named owner.

For a draft-only pilot, keep sending in a separate, human-controlled workflow and do not connect the agent to sending tools. Check the chosen product’s actual permissions rather than assuming it separates drafting from sending. If you cannot verify that separation, keep the workflow manual.

sections.heading: Copy this agent handover sheet
paragraphs: Copy these fields into an editable document for your chosen workflow. For example, keep the handover as a one-page working summary, with detailed tool controls in a separate, clearly referenced stop record. This is an original planning template, not a legal compliance form or evidence that your tools enforce the boundaries you write down.

Replace every bracketed field with a decision or an explicit unresolved issue. Mark any unknown permission or control “unverified—pilot blocked”, and name who will check it. A completed draft records your intentions; authorising the pilot requires evidence that the necessary permissions, approval gates and stop controls work in your chosen configuration.

Accountability: [named owner and contact route]. Backup: [named person and contact route]. Pilot start/end dates: [dates]. Supervised operating window: [hours and time zone].

Approved access: [tools, workspace, accounts and connectors]. Approved inputs: [specific datasets, files or folders]. Draft destination: [location]. Do not enter confidential or personal data into unapproved tools.

Permitted operations: read [specified information]; create drafts [specified location]. Prohibited operations: [record changes, source-file overwrites, sending, publishing, purchasing and other external actions]. Actual permission evidence: [reference or unverified—pilot blocked].

Logging: [location and authorised readers]. Record [item identifier, time, workflow version, outcome, reviewer decision, tool activity, errors and cost], without unnecessary personal information.

Stop and fallback: stop for [privacy concerns, unexpected access/actions, failed controls or exceeded limits]. Who may stop: [names]. Tool-specific stop record: [location/version, operator, verified controls for triggers, queued/active work and connection access, and logs/destinations to inspect]. Manual fallback: [workflow and responsible person].
Restart: only [named authority] may approve after [cause corrected, completed actions checked, pending work reconciled and controls rechecked]. Stopping does not undo completed actions.

blocks.purpose: Make the most consequential misconception visible immediately before the reader writes the stop procedure.
blocks.brief: Use two short sentences to state that telling an agent 'stop' is not a reliable way to remove tool access, and that stopping does not undo completed actions. Direct attention to the tool controls and recovery record that follow; do not imply a universal kill switch. Keep these warnings here rather than repeating them verbatim in nearby prose.

props.text: Telling an agent “stop” does not reliably remove tool access; use verified workflow and account controls. Stopping does not undo completed actions, so record what happened and what recovery requires.

blocks.purpose: The verification order matters: establish actual access before exercising the workflow, rehearse containment before launch, and make readiness a recorded decision.
blocks.brief: Write four ordered, action-led checks as unperformed reader instructions. First, inspect the actual accounts, connector scopes, data locations and approval settings with the owner and backup; compare them with the sheet. Second, use dummy or approved non-sensitive inputs in an isolated setting to check permitted drafting, out-of-scope escalation and absence of send or record-change authority; confirm that withheld approval prevents any gated action. Third, rehearse the stop record by pausing intake, holding queued work, addressing active runs, disabling relevant connections where supported and inspecting logs and destinations; record limitations without treating non-execution alone as proof of denied access. Fourth, record expected and observed results, resolve discrepancies and obtain named authorisation before beginning the bounded pilot. If any necessary control cannot be verified, remain manual. Do not describe these checks as already passed.

layout.rationale: No example-page statistics were supplied, so the article shape follows the complete reader task rather than an invented length benchmark. The 2,060-word target covers section content, including the copyable template and filled example; optional block copy is additional. Paragraph targets refer to explanatory prose, not individual template fields. Use only a critical warning and one ordered verification checklist. Keep the template ungated in the body, honouring feedback to remove generic resource and template CTAs. Omit stock imagery, audience grids and pull quotes because they do not help this single audience complete the handover. Separate the two blocks with substantive prose, and do not plan any automatically rendered hero, navigation, references, disclaimer, company CTA, author or footer components.

claim_bindings.support_excerpt:
Your business is responsible for everything your AI tools do. To protect yourself and your customers, make someone high up in your business accountable for AI safety.

If have a lot of AI tools, you can also assign people to look after individual AI systems.

claim_bindings.claim_text: An AI agent is software that uses information to choose steps towards a goal, sometimes through connected tools.
claim_bindings.support_excerpt:
An autonomous AI agent is a system designed to make decisions and take actions within a defined environment with little or no human intervention.

Unlike traditional AI assistants that respond to single prompts (for example, generating a code snippet), autonomous agents can:

Break down complex goals into smaller tasks

Use external tools (APIs, databases, CI/CD systems)

Monitor outcomes and adjust their behavior

Continue operating without constant human intervention

Business.gov.au advises checking AI-generated information against trustworthy sources before relying on it.
claim_bindings.support_excerpt: However, don't assume that an AI summary is 100% accurate. Always check AI-generated information against a trustworthy source before you rely on it.

claim_bindings.claim_text: Build that review into the handover rather than leaving it as an informal expectation.
Write permissions as separate decisions in your handover.
Reading means viewing approved information, such as a public FAQ.
Drafting means creating proposed text in an approved output location.
Changing means editing an existing business record.
Acting externally means sending a message, publishing content or making a purchase.
These are planning categories, not a claim about how any particular product divides its controls.
Permission to read information does not grant permission to change it, and permission to draft a reply does not grant permission to send it.
Replace broad wording such as “access to customer service” with the actual account, connected tool, dataset or folder and the allowed operation.
Give the agent only the access its task needs.
OpenAI Academy’s small-business workshop advises checking the intended account or workspace, providing only necessary information and keeping a person responsible before acting.
claim_bindings.support_excerpt:
Confirm that you are using the intended account or workspace.

Provide only the information the task requires.

Keep passwords, payment details, confidential records, and other secrets out.

Use public, synthetic, aggregated, or properly de-identified information when possible.

Before you send, publish, schedule, purchase, hire, or make a decision:

Trace important claims to a source.

Check names, dates, prices, policies, and promises.

Keep a person responsible for the final decision.

claim_bindings.claim_text: Its suggested prompt boundaries include keeping work as a draft and flagging missing information.
claim_bindings.support_excerpt: Add one important boundary, such as “flag missing information,” “keep this as a draft,” or “do not invent details.” You can also ask ChatGPT what information is still missing.

claim_bindings.claim_text: Those instructions express your intent; they do not demonstrate that tool permissions enforce it.
Name the reviewer and backup, what they must check, where their decision is recorded and what prevents action without approval.
For a customer-reply draft, require the reviewer to check factual claims against the approved source and check any promises before release.
Record approval against the particular draft reviewed.
If approval is missing or the source cannot answer the question, leave the work pending and refer it to the named owner.
For a draft-only pilot, keep sending in a separate, human-controlled workflow and do not connect the agent to sending tools.
Check the chosen product’s actual permissions rather than assuming it separates drafting from sending.
If you cannot verify that separation, keep the workflow manual.
Copy these fields into an editable document for your chosen workflow.
For example, keep the handover as a one-page working summary, with detailed tool controls in a separate, clearly referenced stop record.
This is an original planning template, not a legal compliance form or evidence that your tools enforce the boundaries you write down.
Replace every bracketed field with a decision or an explicit unresolved issue.
Mark any unknown permission or control “unverified—pilot blocked”, and name who will check it.
A completed draft records your intentions; authorising the pilot requires evidence that the necessary permissions, approval gates and stop controls work in your chosen configuration.
Purpose and scope: [business task and intended output]. Exclusions: [tasks, decisions and information outside scope]. Workflow name/version: [identifier].
Accountability: [named owner and contact route]. Backup: [named person and contact route]. Pilot start/end dates: [dates]. Supervised operating window: [hours and time zone].

Approved access: [tools, workspace, accounts and connectors]. Approved inputs: [specific datasets, files or folders]. Draft destination: [location]. Do not enter confidential or personal data into unapproved tools.

Permitted operations: read [specified information]; create drafts [specified location]. Prohibited operations: [record changes, source-file overwrites, sending, publishing, purchasing and other external actions]. Actual permission evidence: [reference or unverified—pilot blocked].

Approval gate: [named reviewer] checks [facts, source accuracy and commitments]. Approval is recorded in [location]. Without approval: [hold behaviour and technical control preventing further action]. Any human sending occurs through [separate human-controlled workflow].
Escalation: missing facts, uncertainty or out-of-scope work go to [person/contact route]. While awaiting a decision: [hold or manual handling].

Operating limits: maximum run time [duration]; task volume [cap]; retries [cap]; total spending [A$ amount and included charges]. For each limit, record [enforced control or named supervisor and checking schedule]. Alerts alone do not enforce a cap.
Logging: [location and authorised readers]. Record [item identifier, time, workflow version, outcome, reviewer decision, tool activity, errors and cost], without unnecessary personal information.

Stop and fallback: stop for [privacy concerns, unexpected access/actions, failed controls or exceeded limits]. Who may stop: [names]. Tool-specific stop record: [location/version, operator, verified controls for triggers, queued/active work and connection access, and logs/destinations to inspect]. Manual fallback: [workflow and responsible person].
Restart: only [named authority] may approve after [cause corrected, completed actions checked, pending work reconciled and controls rechecked]. Stopping does not undo completed actions.

Pilot decision: manual baseline [location/status]. Measures [end-to-end handling time, quality/corrections and actual costs]. Human review [reviewer and required checks]. Continue if [conditions]; revise if [contained shortfall]; stop if [critical failure or limit breach].

Verification and sign-off: permission checks [status/evidence]; approval checks [status/evidence]; stop rehearsal [status/evidence]. Unresolved issues [issue, owner, follow-up date and launch-blocking status]. Draft reviewed by [owner/backup/date]. Pilot authorisation [pending or named approver/date].
Hypothetical teaching example—not implemented or tested.
This completed planning draft uses invented names, resource labels, limits and decision thresholds.
They are assumptions for the exercise, not customer results, verified product capabilities or recommended benchmarks.
Every proposed technical control remains “unverified—pilot blocked” until checked in the chosen tools.
Purpose and accountability: The fictional workflow, Enquiry Draft Pilot, version A, prepares replies about public opening hours and services.
Maya Chen is the accountable owner; Leo Tran is the backup.
They supervise operation and use their internal team contact channel for escalation.
Account enquiries, complaints, refunds and personalised commitments are outside scope.
Missing facts and out-of-scope requests go to Maya, or Leo when Maya is unavailable, without an invented answer.
Tools and data: The proposed business-approved workflow runner, Draft Runner, reads Public FAQ and Approved Inputs, then creates drafts in Draft Review.
These are fictional resource labels, not vendor menu paths.
Inputs are limited to dummy questions or staff-written, approved non-sensitive summaries.
The agent receives no customer-mailbox access.
Confidential or personal data must not enter unapproved tools.
Permissions and approval: The proposed access allows reading the FAQ and admitted inputs and creating new drafts in Draft Review.
It prohibits sending, publishing, purchasing, changing customer records, overwriting source files and using unapproved tools.
Maya or Leo checks every draft against the FAQ and records approval, required changes or rejection in Review Log.
Without approval, the draft stays unused.
A person may manually send an approved reply from a separate mail application.
The agent has no sending connector, and that separation must be verified before launch.

Operating limits: In this hypothetical pilot, operation lasts five working days from an authorised start, covers at most 20 eligible enquiries and permits one draft attempt per enquiry, with an A$30 tool-cost ceiling.
Maya records the start and end dates when authorising launch.
Operation is supervised only.
The proposed runner configuration would enforce the end date, task count and no-retry rule; Maya or Leo would control each operating session.
A provider-side spending cap would need verification.
Cost alerts alone would not establish an enforced ceiling.
Any limit without a workable, verified enforcement or supervision method remains a launch blocker.
Logging and escalation: Review Log is restricted to Maya and Leo and records the item ID, time, workflow version, draft outcome, reviewer decision, tool activity and cost.
It avoids unnecessary customer information.
Either operator may stop the workflow for suspected data exposure, unexpected access, prohibited activity, failed controls or exceeded limits.
Maya alone may authorise restart after correction, reconciliation of pending work and repeated checks.
Stop record: Stop Map A identifies Draft Runner, the Approved Inputs pending-work area, and the Public FAQ and Draft Review connections.
Maya is the primary stop operator and proposed connection administrator; Leo is the backup, subject to verifying that both have the necessary access.
The intended procedure is to pause submissions and triggers, hold queued items, check active runs separately, and disable relevant connections where supported and safe.
They would inspect runner activity, pending items, draft history and billing records for completed actions, outstanding work and charges.
Exact control locations, shared-account dependencies and effects on queued and active work still require verification using current provider instructions.
Uncertain control or output integrity means switching to manual drafting and review.
Pilot decision: Before launch, Maya records a comparable manual baseline for end-to-end handling time, factual quality and cost.
Assisted handling time includes preparation, review, corrections and manual sending; setup and rehearsal effort are recorded separately for the overall assessment.
The hypothetical continue rule requires lower reviewed handling time, no material factual errors or boundary breaches, and costs within the ceiling.
A contained quality or time shortfall calls for revision and another agreed scope.
Privacy, permission or control failures require stopping.
Continuing does not grant sending authority.
Verification and sign-off: The draft is complete.
Permission checks, the baseline and the stop rehearsal are pending.
The pilot is not authorised.
Write down which person will operate the actual workflow and account controls, and how they will check the result.
Attach a compact stop map to the handover for each connected tool.

Record its tool and workflow identifier, responsible operator and required access, verified control location, treatment of queued and active work, connection-disable method, evidence to inspect, manual fallback and restart condition.
This guide provides a planning checklist, not vendor-specific stop instructions.
Fill in these details from your administration screens and current provider instructions, then verify them before launch.
If a necessary control remains unverified, keep the workflow manual.
The owner or backup should record the stop trigger and time, then pause new manual submissions, schedules and event triggers.
Hold or cancel queued work using the controls documented in the stop map.
Check active runs separately and establish whether the tool supports cancelling them.
Do not treat paused intake as evidence that work already running has stopped.
The authorised administrator should then disable the relevant workflow connection, integration account or access credential where the product supports it and it is safe to do so.
Identify shared-account dependencies before the pilot so the administrator knows what else a change could interrupt.
Verify the effect in the connected tools rather than assuming that revoking access instantly cancels every operation.
Inspect available workflow logs and destination tools for completed actions, outstanding jobs, duplicate work and charges.
Preserve the incident record, including what the operator checked and found.
Where logs are incomplete, record the uncertainty and escalate it to the accountable owner rather than concluding that nothing happened.
Switch to the documented manual workflow whenever control or output integrity is uncertain.
Any correction of a completed action needs its own authorisation.
Restart only after the cause has been addressed and pending work has been reconciled.
Repeat the relevant permission and stop checks, and obtain approval from the named restart authority before resuming.
Record that decision in the handover.
Ask your administrator to show what actually prevents an unapproved action, and confirm that the owner and backup can access the controls they are expected to operate.
Use dummy or approved non-sensitive data in an isolated test setting for permission checks and the stop rehearsal.
Do not attempt prohibited actions against real customers, live business records or payment destinations.
Keep a verification record alongside the handover.
Describe what you observed rather than simply writing ‘passed’, and assign each unresolved issue to someone who can follow it up.
A successful rehearsal provides limited evidence for that configuration, not a safety guarantee.
Before the pilot begins, record how your team handles comparable eligible tasks manually: end-to-end handling time, corrections or quality issues, and relevant costs.
This is your baseline for deciding whether the assisted workflow helps.
For the customer-enquiry teaching example, the baseline still needs to be measured; no time saving has been established.
Add the pilot end date, task-volume ceiling, supervised operating window and budget in A$ to the handover.
For each limit, record whether the tool stops execution or merely alerts someone.
An alert needs a named person to act on it and is not an enforced spending cap.
Measure the whole assisted workflow, not just how quickly the agent produces text.
Include preparing the input, checking the draft, correcting it and sending the approved reply manually.
Record setup and stop-rehearsal effort separately, then include that effort in the overall pilot assessment.
Alongside handling time, log factual errors, corrections, escalations and any action outside the agreed permissions.
Track actual tool costs, including relevant subscription and usage charges.
Keep human review throughout: a draft-only pilot still requires someone to check every reply against the approved information before using it.
Write the continue, revise and stop rules before launch, so faster drafting cannot quietly outweigh a control failure.
Continue only when the agreed time, quality and cost conditions are met and no critical issue remains unresolved.
Revise a contained quality or time shortfall by documenting the change, agreeing a new scope and repeating the relevant checks before resuming.

Stop for uncontrolled access, privacy concerns, failed stop controls or exceeded operating limits, and follow the handover’s stop-and-recovery procedure rather than simply asking the agent to behave differently.
At the review date, use the recorded results to decide the next step.
A small pilot provides evidence about that workflow under those conditions, not proof of general productivity gains.
If you continue, retain the existing permissions unless a separate review explicitly authorises a change.
Better draft performance does not, by itself, justify connecting a sending tool or removing human approval.
Have the owner and backup review and date the handover draft.
Take a sanitised summary to peers, with the unresolved decisions clearly marked.
Leave out credentials, customer messages and confidential workflow details.
Peer discussion can help you spot missing questions, but it does not replace checking the actual configuration with the person who administers your tools.
Adapt these questions to the decisions still open in your draft:
Can our chosen tools separate drafting from sending, and what evidence should we ask the administrator to show?
What happens to queued and active work when our stop controls are used?
Which quality failures should stop this pilot even if handling time improves?
You can explore MLAI events to learn alongside other builders and business owners.
Check a relevant event page before deciding to attend: availability, format and cost depend on that page.
Attendance does not guarantee individual implementation advice or replace permission checks, the stop rehearsal or pilot preparation.

06Before we start
Common
questions.
Bring your questions to your free 15-minute chat with Sam.
Do I need to know what I want built?
No. You can show us a task that takes too long, or describe an idea. We’ll work out with you whether there’s a project worth doing.
Why not just use an existing AI tool?
You might not need a custom build. We’ll check what your existing tools can do first. New software is an option when those tools can’t do the job or need to work together.
Can you work with the software we already use?
We’ll check how your software can connect to other systems and what access we’d need. That tells us what’s possible before we quote.
What about sensitive data?
Tell us what restrictions apply before sending any sensitive data. The proposal will set out who can access it and where it will be processed and stored. If it must stay in Australia, raise that in the first conversation.
Who owns the code and accounts?
After full payment, you own the work made specifically for you, unless your agreement says otherwise. MLAI keeps ownership of its pre-existing tools, reusable components and other background IP. Third-party software has its own licences. We agree account access, billing and handover in the proposal.
What happens after launch?
We’ll agree how the software is handed over and whether you need ongoing support. Maintenance and further changes are quoted separately unless your agreement includes them.
How long will it take?
We can give you a timeline once we’ve looked at the scope and the systems involved. The proposal includes milestones so you know when to expect work to review.
